destination.title: The Day $1 Trillion Vanished in 36 Minutes

short18: In thirty-six minutes, almost a trillion dollars vanished from the U.S.
The market fell nearly a thousand points in minutes, and famous shares briefly traded for a penny.
Investigators traced part of the imbalance to a trader in a London bedroom, flashing giant orders he meant to cancel.
He pleaded guilty to spoofing and wire fraud, but not to causing the crash.
No account blames one man alone: a four-billion-dollar sell order and panicking machines were part of it too.
Watch the full story on the channel.

candidate_payload_lines: It is about a machine so fast and so clever that almost no one fully understood it — and how close that machine came to falling apart, in front of everyone, in the middle of an ordinary afternoon.
But here is the truth underneath that promise, the one almost nobody likes to say out loud.
Which raises a dangerous question, one that, in twenty-ten, almost no one was asking out loud.

What if you could show the machines something that wasn't true — a flood of buyers that didn't exist, a wall of sellers who were never really there — and simply let their own speed and logic do the rest?
Orders that were never, for one moment, meant to be filled.
In the blink of an eye, the orders that frightened the whole market simply vanish — because they were never meant to be filled.
The wall goes up, the wall comes down, and only the man who built it ever knows it was never really there.
For most of those years, almost no one even notices.
The only question left — the one nobody has thought to ask — is what happens if, one day, he leans on it at exactly the wrong moment.
The machines that promised to always be there do the one thing no one had planned for, the one thing the whole system quietly depended on them never doing.
If a system this powerful can be pushed to the edge of collapse by a lie told in orders that were never even real — then what, exactly, broke that day?
He had beaten the high score, over and over, for years — and kept almost none of the points.

The truth is smaller, and sadder: a brilliant, lonely man, chasing a number on a screen, who understood the rule he broke better than almost anyone — and never seemed to grasp, or to care, what the number was actually worth.

shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: The market came back inside an hour. So why did it take five years to work out what had pushed it?

lines.text: Two thirty-two in the afternoon. The machines that promised to always be there did the one thing no one had planned for. They stepped back. All at once.
source_lines: The machines that promised to always be there do the one thing no one had planned for, the one thing the whole system quietly depended on them never doing.
They step back. All at once.

lines.text: To protect themselves from a falling market, they simply stopped buying. And the floor disappeared.
source_lines: To protect themselves from a falling market, they simply stop buying. And the floor disappears.

lines.text: All over the country, ordinary people had left standing instructions with their brokers. Sell automatically if my stock falls below this price. Small, sensible safety nets meant to protect them.
source_lines: All over the country, ordinary people have left standing instructions with their brokers — sell, automatically, if my stock ever falls below this price — small, sensible safety nets meant to protect them.

lines.text: In those thirty-six minutes those instructions fired, all at once, selling people's savings into the very bottom of the crash, at the worst prices of the day.
source_lines: In those thirty-six minutes, as prices fall through the floor, those instructions fire, all at once, selling people's savings into the very bottom of the crash, at the worst prices of the day.

lines.text: With almost no machines left to catch them, shares in giant, healthy companies plunged toward nothing.
source_lines: With almost no machines left willing to catch them, shares in giant, healthy, world-famous companies plunge toward nothing.

lines.text: For a few seconds a share of a company worth tens of billions traded at a single penny.
source_lines: For a few astonishing seconds, you could have bought a share of a company worth tens of billions of dollars for a single penny
Shares in some of the most famous companies in America trade, for a heartbeat, at a single penny.

lines.text: Nearly a thousand points and around a trillion dollars in value were gone, until circuit breakers fired and the market climbed back.
source_lines: Nearly a thousand points, gone. Around a trillion dollars in value, gone.
Automatic circuit breakers, built for exactly this, begin to fire; exchanges pause; the panic runs out of room.

lines.text: The safety net people set up to protect their savings is what sold those savings at the bottom. It took thirty-six minutes.

shorts.angle: He took tens of millions off the fastest machines on earth, and by the time they arrested him almost all of it had been taken from him.
shorts.type: B - what the money actually bought, which was nothing
shorts.avoids: short18 explains spoofing and the guilty plea. It never touches what happened to the money, why prosecutors asked for mercy, or the sentence he actually received.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: How does one man in a bedroom lean hard enough on the largest market on earth to make it bend?

lines.text: When investigators finally opened up his life, the fortune was mostly gone. Not spent. Taken.
source_lines: is mostly gone. Not spent. Taken.

lines.text: He had handed his money, almost all of it, to con men, to bogus investments, to an outright fraud built to part trusting people from their savings.
source_lines: he had handed his money, almost all of it, to con men, to bogus investments, to an outright fraud built to part trusting people from their savings

lines.text: People who knew him describe a man trading the way a child plays an arcade game. Locked onto the screen, hour after hour, trying to beat his own high score.
source_lines: People who knew him describe a man trading the way a child plays an arcade game — locked onto the screen, hour after hour, trying, over and over, to beat his own high score.

lines.text: He had beaten the high score, over and over, for years, and kept almost none of the points.
source_lines: He had beaten the high score, over and over, for years — and kept almost none of the points.

lines.text: He never bought the cars, the house, or the life the money could buy. A specialist later testified this was not an act.
source_lines: He doesn't buy the cars, or the house, or the life the money could have bought.
An autism specialist will later put it as plainly as it can be put: his lack of any interest in the money he earned was not an act.

lines.text: In 2015 he was arrested at his parents' house in London. He fought the extradition for months and he lost.
source_lines: He is arrested at his parents' house in London
He fights the extradition for months. He loses.

lines.text: In 2016 he pleaded guilty to wire fraud and to spoofing, and agreed to hand back nearly thirteen million dollars.
source_lines: In twenty-sixteen, he pleads guilty.
one count of wire fraud, and one count of spoofing.
He agrees to hand back nearly thirteen million dollars.

lines.text: At his sentencing the prosecutors did something rare. They asked the judge for mercy. He served no further prison at all, a single year at home.
